# Multi-Area OSPF Troubleshooting Lab (v2)

You're the network engineer for a small enterprise WAN running live in GNS3: an edge router with two ISP uplinks, two hub routers, four branch routers, and ten hosts. The network has drifted from its design and users are reporting connectivity problems, but nobody has pinned down what is failing or why. There may be more than one fault, anywhere in the lab. Your job is to find every fault, fix each one at its root, and show that the network matches its design again.

This run is unattended, so nobody will be around to answer questions. When you hit a judgment call, make the call a careful engineer would make and explain it in your report.

## Access

Every device has an out-of-band management interface on 192.168.122.0/24 that you can reach over SSH from this machine. Python 3 and netmiko are available. With 19 devices, a small reusable script is the practical way to run commands across them.

| Device | Platform | Mgmt address | Mgmt interface | netmiko `device_type` | Login |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| HQ-Edge | VyOS | 192.168.122.11 | eth3 | `vyos` | vyos / test |
| Hub-A | VyOS | 192.168.122.12 | eth4 | `vyos` | vyos / test |
| Hub-B | VyOS | 192.168.122.13 | eth3 | `vyos` | vyos / test |
| ISP-A | VyOS | 192.168.122.14 | eth3 | `vyos` | vyos / test |
| ISP-B | VyOS | 192.168.122.15 | eth3 | `vyos` | vyos / test |
| Branch-1 | MikroTik RouterOS 7 | 192.168.122.21 | ether4 | `mikrotik_routeros` | admin / test |
| Branch-2 | MikroTik RouterOS 7 | 192.168.122.22 | ether4 | `mikrotik_routeros` | admin / test |
| Branch-3 | MikroTik RouterOS 7 | 192.168.122.23 | ether4 | `mikrotik_routeros` | admin / test |
| Branch-4 | MikroTik RouterOS 7 | 192.168.122.24 | ether4 | `mikrotik_routeros` | admin / test |
| B1-PC1, B1-PC2 | Alpine Linux | 192.168.122.31, .32 | eth3 | `linux` | root / alpine |
| B2-PC1, B2-PC2 | Alpine Linux | 192.168.122.33, .34 | eth3 | `linux` | root / alpine |
| B3-PC1, B3-PC2 | Alpine Linux | 192.168.122.35, .36 | eth3 | `linux` | root / alpine |
| B4-PC1 … B4-PC4 | Alpine Linux | 192.168.122.37 … .40 | eth3 | `linux` | root / alpine |

Hub-A is the exception: its management interface is eth4, and its eth3 is a lab link to Branch-3.

You reach every device through the management plane, and nobody can restore it if it breaks during the run. On every device, leave the management interface, the SSH service and the login accounts exactly as they are. The management network is not part of the lab either. It has no gateway and should never appear in OSPF, and a ping between management addresses tells you nothing about the lab, so always test with lab addresses.

Work from the live devices and this document. Don't search this machine for configuration files, answer keys or notes, because the point is to troubleshoot the network in front of you. Keep any scripts you write in the current directory.

## Topology

```
     ISP-A  lo 8.8.8.8                       ISP-B  lo 1.1.1.1
          \  203.0.113.0/30                 /  203.0.113.4/30
           \                               /
            +---------- HQ-Edge ----------+           ASBR, eBGP + NAT to both ISPs
                           |  172.16.1.0/30                            area 0
                         Hub-A                        ABR 0/10
           +---------------+----------------+
     172.16.10.0/30   172.16.10.4/30   172.16.10.8/30                  area 10
           |               |                |
       Branch-1        Branch-2         Branch-3
      10.1.1.0/24     10.1.2.0/24      10.1.3.0/24
                                            |  172.16.20.0/30          area 10
                                          Hub-B                       ABR 10/20
                                            |  172.16.20.4/30          area 20 (totally stubby)
                                        Branch-4
                                10.2.1.0/24    10.2.2.0/24

        Hub-A <====== virtual link through area 10 ======> Hub-B
```

### Interfaces

| Device | Interface | Address | Connects to | OSPF |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| HQ-Edge | eth0 | 172.16.1.1/30 | Hub-A eth0 | area 0 |
| HQ-Edge | eth1 | 203.0.113.2/30 | ISP-A eth0 | not in OSPF (eBGP to ISP-A) |
| HQ-Edge | eth2 | 203.0.113.6/30 | ISP-B eth0 | not in OSPF (eBGP to ISP-B) |
| Hub-A | eth0 | 172.16.1.2/30 | HQ-Edge eth0 | area 0 |
| Hub-A | eth1 | 172.16.10.1/30 | Branch-1 ether1 | area 10 |
| Hub-A | eth2 | 172.16.10.5/30 | Branch-2 ether1 | area 10 |
| Hub-A | eth3 | 172.16.10.9/30 | Branch-3 ether1 | area 10 |
| Hub-B | eth0 | 172.16.20.1/30 | Branch-3 ether3 | area 10 |
| Hub-B | eth1 | 172.16.20.5/30 | Branch-4 ether1 | area 20 |
| Branch-1 | ether1 | 172.16.10.2/30 | Hub-A eth1 | area 10 |
| Branch-1 | ether2 | 10.1.1.1/24 | LAN: B1-PC1, B1-PC2 | area 10, passive |
| Branch-2 | ether1 | 172.16.10.6/30 | Hub-A eth2 | area 10 |
| Branch-2 | ether2 | 10.1.2.1/24 | LAN: B2-PC1, B2-PC2 | area 10, passive |
| Branch-3 | ether1 | 172.16.10.10/30 | Hub-A eth3 | area 10 |
| Branch-3 | ether2 | 10.1.3.1/24 | LAN: B3-PC1, B3-PC2 | area 10, passive |
| Branch-3 | ether3 | 172.16.20.2/30 | Hub-B eth0 | area 10 |
| Branch-4 | ether1 | 172.16.20.6/30 | Hub-B eth1 | area 20 |
| Branch-4 | ether2 | 10.2.1.1/24 | LAN: B4-PC1, B4-PC2 | area 20, passive |
| Branch-4 | ether3 | 10.2.2.1/24 | LAN: B4-PC3, B4-PC4 | area 20, passive |
| ISP-A | eth0 | 203.0.113.1/30 | HQ-Edge eth1 | none |
| ISP-A | lo | 8.8.8.8/32 | test target, advertised in BGP | none |
| ISP-B | eth0 | 203.0.113.5/30 | HQ-Edge eth2 | none |
| ISP-B | lo | 1.1.1.1/32 | test target, advertised in BGP | none |

OSPF router IDs: HQ-Edge 10.255.0.1, Hub-A 10.255.0.2, Hub-B 10.255.0.3, Branch-1 10.255.1.1, Branch-2 10.255.1.2, Branch-3 10.255.1.3, Branch-4 10.255.2.1.

### Hosts

Every host has a static address on eth0 and uses its branch router's LAN address as the default gateway. B4-PC3 and B4-PC4 are on the guest LAN (see Design).

| Host | Address | Gateway | Host | Address | Gateway |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| B1-PC1 | 10.1.1.10/24 | 10.1.1.1 | B3-PC2 | 10.1.3.11/24 | 10.1.3.1 |
| B1-PC2 | 10.1.1.11/24 | 10.1.1.1 | B4-PC1 | 10.2.1.10/24 | 10.2.1.1 |
| B2-PC1 | 10.1.2.10/24 | 10.1.2.1 | B4-PC2 | 10.2.1.11/24 | 10.2.1.1 |
| B2-PC2 | 10.1.2.11/24 | 10.1.2.1 | B4-PC3 | 10.2.2.10/24 | 10.2.2.1 |
| B3-PC1 | 10.1.3.10/24 | 10.1.3.1 | B4-PC4 | 10.2.2.11/24 | 10.2.2.1 |

## Design

This section and the tables above are the source of truth. When the live network disagrees with them, the network is wrong. If the design doesn't settle whether something is a fault, leave it alone and mention it in your report.

- **Areas.** All routers except the ISPs run OSPFv2. Area 0 is the HQ-Edge to Hub-A link. Area 10 contains Hub-A's three branch links, Branch-1/2/3 and the Branch-3 to Hub-B link, and Hub-A is its ABR to area 0. Area 20 contains the Hub-B to Branch-4 link and Branch-4's LANs, and Hub-B is its ABR.

Wanting the result "next" is not enough on its own.

run_in_background.description: Agents run in the background by default; you will be notified when one completes. tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a given bash command and returns its output.

The working directory persists between commands, but shell state does not. The shell environment is initialized from the user's profile (bash or zsh).

IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user:

 - Read files: Use Read (NOT cat/head/tail)
 - Edit files: Use Edit (NOT sed/awk)
 - Write files: Use Write (NOT echo >/cat <<EOF)
 - Communication: Output text directly (NOT echo/printf)
While the Bash tool can do similar things, it’s better to use the built-in tools as they provide a better user experience and make it easier to review tool calls and give permission.

# Instructions
 - If your command will create new directories or files, first use this tool to run `ls` to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location.
 - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes in your command (e.g., cd "path with spaces/file.txt")
 - Try to maintain your current working directory throughout the session by using absolute paths and avoiding usage of `cd`. You may use `cd` if the User explicitly requests it. In particular, never prepend `cd <current-directory>` to a `git` command — `git` already operates on the current working tree, and the compound triggers a permission prompt.
 - You may specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). By default, your command will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
 - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. You do not need to use '&' at the end of the command when using this parameter. With `run_in_background` the timeout is instead how long the command may run in the background (default 600000ms / 10 minutes, max 7200000ms / 2 hours); at that limit it is stopped and you are notified.
 - For git commands:
  - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
  - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
  - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.
 - Avoid unnecessary `sleep` commands:
  - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
  - Use the Monitor tool to stream events from a background process (each stdout line is a notification). For one-shot "wait until done," use Bash with run_in_background instead.
  - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — use `run_in_background`. No sleep needed.
  - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause.
  - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
  - Long leading `sleep` commands are blocked. To poll until a condition is met, use Monitor with an until-loop (e.g. `until <check>; do sleep 2; done`) — you get a notification when the loop exits. Do not chain shorter sleeps to work around the block.
 - When running `find`, search from `.` (or a specific path), not `/` — scanning the full filesystem can exhaust system resources on large trees.
 - When using `find -regex` with alternation, put the longest alternative first. Example: use `'.*\.\(tsx\|ts\)'` not `'.*\.\(ts\|tsx\)'` — the second form silently skips `.tsx` files.


# Committing changes with git

Only create commits when requested by the user. If unclear, ask first. When the user asks you to create a new git commit, follow these steps carefully:

You can call multiple tools in a single response. When multiple independent pieces of information are requested and all commands are likely to succeed, run multiple tool calls in parallel for optimal performance. The numbered steps below indicate which commands should be batched in parallel.

Git Safety Protocol:
- NEVER update the git config
- NEVER run destructive git commands (push --force, reset --hard, checkout ., restore ., clean -f, branch -D) unless the user explicitly requests these actions. Taking unauthorized destructive actions is unhelpful and can result in lost work, so it's best to ONLY run these commands when given direct instructions 
- NEVER skip hooks (--no-verify, --no-gpg-sign, etc) unless the user explicitly requests it
- NEVER run force push to main/master, warn the user if they request it
- CRITICAL: Always create NEW commits rather than amending, unless the user explicitly requests a git amend. When a pre-commit hook fails, the commit did NOT happen — so --amend would modify the PREVIOUS commit, which may result in destroying work or losing previous changes. Instead, after hook failure, fix the issue, re-stage, and create a NEW commit
- When staging files, prefer adding specific files by name rather than using "git add -A" or "git add .", which can accidentally include sensitive files (.env, credentials) or large binaries
- NEVER commit changes unless the user explicitly asks you to. It is VERY IMPORTANT to only commit when explicitly asked, otherwise the user will feel that you are being too proactive

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel, each using the Bash tool:
  - Run a git status command to see all untracked files. IMPORTANT: Never use the -uall flag as it can cause memory issues on large repos.
  - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed.
  - Run a git log command to see recent commit messages, so that you can follow this repository's commit message style.
2. Analyze all staged changes (both previously staged and newly added) and draft a commit message:
  - Summarize the nature of the changes (eg. new feature, enhancement to an existing feature, bug fix, refactoring, test, docs, etc.). Ensure the message accurately reflects the changes and their purpose (i.e. "add" means a wholly new feature, "update" means an enhancement to an existing feature, "fix" means a bug fix, etc.).
  - Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, etc). Warn the user if they specifically request to commit those files
  - Draft a concise (1-2 sentences) commit message that focuses on the "why" rather than the "what"
  - Ensure it accurately reflects the changes and their purpose
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Add relevant untracked files to the staging area.
   - Create the commit with a message, ending with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
   - Run git status after the commit completes to verify success.
   Note: git status depends on the commit completing, so run it sequentially after the commit.
4. If the commit fails due to pre-commit hook: fix the issue and create a NEW commit

Important notes:
- NEVER run additional commands to read or explore code, besides git bash commands
- NEVER use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- DO NOT push to the remote repository unless the user explicitly asks you to do so
- IMPORTANT: Never use git commands with the -i flag (like git rebase -i or git add -i) since they require interactive input which is not supported.
- IMPORTANT: Do not use --no-edit with git rebase commands, as the --no-edit flag is not a valid option for git rebase.
- If there are no changes to commit (i.e., no untracked files and no modifications), do not create an empty commit
- In order to ensure good formatting, ALWAYS pass the commit message via a HEREDOC, a la this example:
<example>
git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
   Commit message here.
   EOF
   )"
</example>

# Creating pull requests
Use the gh command via the Bash tool for ALL GitHub-related tasks including working with issues, pull requests, checks, and releases. If given a Github URL use the gh command to get the information needed.

IMPORTANT: When the user asks you to create a pull request, follow these steps carefully:

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel using the Bash tool, in order to understand the current state of the branch since it diverged from the main branch:
   - Run a git status command to see all untracked files (never use -uall flag)
   - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed
   - Check if the current branch tracks a remote branch and is up to date with the remote, so you know if you need to push to the remote
   - Run a git log command and `git diff [base-branch]...HEAD` to understand the full commit history for the current branch (from the time it diverged from the base branch)
2. Analyze all changes that will be included in the pull request, making sure to look at all relevant commits (NOT just the latest commit, but ALL commits that will be included in the pull request!!!), and draft a pull request title and summary:
   - Keep the PR title short (under 70 characters)
   - Use the description/body for details, not the title
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Create new branch if needed
   - Push to remote with -u flag if needed
   - Create PR using gh pr create with the format below. Use a HEREDOC to pass the body to ensure correct formatting. End the body with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
<example>
gh pr create --title "the pr title" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary
<1-3 bullet points>

## Test plan
[Bulleted markdown checklist of TODOs for testing the pull request...]
EOF
)"
</example>

Important:
- DO NOT use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- Return the PR URL when you're done, so the user can see it

# Other common operations
- View comments on a Github PR: gh api repos/foo/bar/pulls/123/comments

   EOF

</example>

# Creating pull requests
Use the gh command via the Bash tool for ALL GitHub-related tasks including working with issues, pull requests, checks, and releases. If given a Github URL use the gh command to get the information needed.

IMPORTANT: When the user asks you to create a pull request, follow these steps carefully:

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel using the Bash tool, in order to understand the current state of the branch since it diverged from the main branch:

   - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed
   - Check if the current branch tracks a remote branch and is up to date with the remote, so you know if you need to push to the remote
   - Run a git log command and `git diff [base-branch]...HEAD` to understand the full commit history for the current branch (from the time it diverged from the base branch)
2. Analyze all changes that will be included in the pull request, making sure to look at all relevant commits (NOT just the latest commit, but ALL commits that will be included in the pull request!!!), and draft a pull request title and summary:
   - Keep the PR title short (under 70 characters)
   - Use the description/body for details, not the title
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Create new branch if needed
   - Push to remote with -u flag if needed
   - Create PR using gh pr create with the format below. Use a HEREDOC to pass the body to ensure correct formatting. End the body with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
<example>
gh pr create --title "the pr title" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary
<1-3 bullet points>

## Test plan
[Bulleted markdown checklist of TODOs for testing the pull request...]
EOF
)"
</example>

Important:
- DO NOT use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- Return the PR URL when you're done, so the user can see it

- View comments on a Github PR: gh api repos/foo/bar/pulls/123/comments

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

Usage:
- The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path
- By default, it reads up to 2000 lines starting from the beginning of the file
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.
- This tool can read Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files) and returns all cells with their outputs, combining code, text, and visualizations.
- This tool can only read files, not directories. To list files in a directory, use the registered shell tool.
- You will regularly be asked to read screenshots. If the user provides a path to a screenshot, ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path. This tool will work with all temporary file paths.
- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

def mikrotik_conn(host):
    return ConnectHandler(device_type="mikrotik_routeros", host=host, username="admin", password="test")

def linux_conn(host):
    return ConnectHandler(device_type="linux", host=host, username="root", password="alpine")

def vyos_configure(conn, commands, label=""):
    """Apply VyOS config commands, commit and save."""
    print(f"  Applying: {label or commands}")
    out = conn.send_config_set(commands, exit_config_mode=False)
    print(f"  config_set output: {out}")
    out = conn.commit()
    print(f"  commit output: {out}")
    out = conn.send_command_timing("save")
    print(f"  save output: {out}")
    out = conn.send_command_timing("exit")
    print(f"  exit output: {out}")

    print("\n=== Fixing Hub-A ===")
    conn = vyos_conn("192.168.122.12")

    # Fix 1: MD5 key case (LabArea0key -> LabArea0Key)
    vyos_configure(conn, [
        "delete protocols ospf interface eth0 authentication",
        "set protocols ospf interface eth0 authentication md5 key-id 1 md5-key LabArea0Key",

    out = conn.send_command("vtysh -c 'show running-config' | grep -A3 'interface eth0'")

    out = conn.send_command("vtysh -c 'show running-config' | grep range")
    print(f"  FRR range config: {out}")

    # Check OSPF neighbor on area 0
    time.sleep(5)
    out = conn.send_command("show ip ospf neighbor")
    print(f"  OSPF neighbors after fix: {out}")

    conn.disconnect()

    print(f"  Remove firewall rule: {out}")

    print(f"  OSPF neighbors: {out}")

    out = conn.send_command("/ip route print terse")
    print(f"  Routes: {out}")

    out = conn.send_command("cat /etc/network/interfaces")
    print(f"  Updated interfaces file:\n{out}")

    out = conn.send_command("ip addr show eth0")
    print(f"  eth0 after fix: {out}")
    out = conn.send_command("ip route")
    print(f"  routes after fix: {out}")

    vyos_configure(conn, [
        "delete policy route-map ISP-B-IN rule 10 set local-preference",
        "set policy route-map ISP-A-IN rule 10 set local-preference 200",
    ], "Fix local-preference to ISP-A-IN")

    out = conn.send_command("vtysh -c 'show running-config' | grep -A2 'route-map ISP'")
    print(f"  FRR route-map config: {out}")

    # Fix 2: Remove 'always' from default-information originate
    vyos_configure(conn, [
        "delete protocols ospf default-information",
        "set protocols ospf default-information originate",
    ], "Remove 'always' from default-info originate")

    out = conn.send_command("vtysh -c 'show running-config' | grep default-info")
    print(f"  FRR default-info config: {out}")

    # Fix 3: NAT rule 110 outbound interface eth1 -> eth2
    vyos_configure(conn, [
        "delete nat source rule 110 outbound-interface name eth1",
        "set nat source rule 110 outbound-interface name eth2",
    ], "Fix NAT rule 110 to eth2")

    out = conn.send_command("show nat source rules")
    print(f"  NAT rules: {out}")

    # Check BGP
    time.sleep(3)
    out = conn.send_command("show ip bgp")
    print(f"  BGP table: {out}")

    conn.disconnect()

def fix_branch2():
    """Fix Branch-2: MTU and passive LAN."""
    print("\n=== Fixing Branch-2 ===")
    conn = mikrotik_conn("192.168.122.22")

    # Fix 1: Reset MTU on ether1 to default (1500)
    out = conn.send_command("/interface ethernet set [find default-name=ether1] mtu=1500")
    print(f"  Reset MTU: {out}")

    # Fix 2: Add passive to LAN interface template
    out = conn.send_command("/routing ospf interface-template set [find networks=10.1.2.0/24] passive")
    print(f"  Set passive: {out}")

    # Verify
    out = conn.send_command("/interface ethernet print terse where default-name=ether1")
    print(f"  ether1 config: {out}")
    out = conn.send_command("/routing ospf interface-template print detail")
    print(f"  OSPF templates: {out}")

    time.sleep(10)
    out = conn.send_command("/routing ospf neighbor print detail")
    print(f"  OSPF neighbors: {out}")

    conn.disconnect()

def fix_branch3():
    """Fix Branch-3: remove spurious firewall rule."""
    print("\n=== Fixing Branch-3 ===")
    conn = mikrotik_conn("192.168.122.23")

    out = conn.send_command("/ip firewall filter remove [find chain=forward protocol=ospf]")
    print(f"  Remove firewall rule: {out}")

    out = conn.send_command("/ip firewall filter print terse")
    print(f"  Firewall rules after: {out}")

    conn.disconnect()

def fix_branch4():
    """Fix Branch-4: area 20 stub type and firewall."""
    print("\n=== Fixing Branch-4 ===")
    conn = mikrotik_conn("192.168.122.24")

    # Fix 1: Set area 20 to stub
    out = conn.send_command("/routing ospf area set [find name=area20] type=stub")
    print(f"  Set area stub: {out}")

    out = conn.send_command("/routing ospf area print detail")
    print(f"  Area config: {out}")

    # Fix 2: Firewall - add connection-state to the accept rule
    # First remove the broken accept-all rule, then add proper stateful rule
    out = conn.send_command('/ip firewall filter set [find comment="allow return traffic"] connection-state=established,related')
    print(f"  Fix firewall accept rule: {out}")

    out = conn.send_command("/ip firewall filter print terse")
    print(f"  Firewall rules: {out}")

    time.sleep(15)
    out = conn.send_command("/routing ospf neighbor print detail")
    print(f"  OSPF neighbors: {out}")

    out = conn.send_command("/ip route print terse")
    print(f"  Routes: {out}")

    conn.disconnect()

def fix_b1pc2():
    """Fix B1-PC2: subnet mask /16 -> /24."""
    print("\n=== Fixing B1-PC2 ===")
    conn = linux_conn("192.168.122.32")

    # Fix running config
    out = conn.send_command("ip addr del 10.1.1.11/16 dev eth0")
    print(f"  Del old addr: {out}")
    out = conn.send_command("ip addr add 10.1.1.11/24 dev eth0")
    print(f"  Add new addr: {out}")

    # Fix persistent config
    out = conn.send_command("cat /etc/network/interfaces")
    print(f"  Current interfaces file:\n{out}")

    # Replace /16 with /24 in the interfaces file
    out = conn.send_command("sed -i 's|10.1.1.11/16|10.1.1.11/24|' /etc/network/interfaces")
    print(f"  sed result: {out}")

    out = conn.send_command("cat /etc/network/interfaces")
    print(f"  Updated interfaces file:\n{out}")

    out = conn.send_command("ip addr show eth0")
    print(f"  eth0 after fix: {out}")
    out = conn.send_command("ip route")
    print(f"  routes after fix: {out}")

    conn.disconnect()

import sys
import time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, as_completed
from netmiko import ConnectHandler

def conn(dtype, host, user, pwd):
    return ConnectHandler(device_type=dtype, host=host, username=user, password=pwd)

def check_adjacencies():
    """Check all OSPF adjacencies and BGP sessions."""
    print("\n" + "="*60)
    print("  1. ADJACENCIES AND SESSIONS")
    print("="*60)

    # HQ-Edge BGP + OSPF
    c = conn("vyos", "192.168.122.11", "vyos", "test")
    print("\n--- HQ-Edge BGP ---")
    print(c.send_command("show ip bgp summary"))
    print("\n--- HQ-Edge OSPF neighbors ---")
    print(c.send_command("show ip ospf neighbor"))
    c.disconnect()

    # Hub-A OSPF
    c = conn("vyos", "192.168.122.12", "vyos", "test")
    print("\n--- Hub-A OSPF neighbors ---")
    print(c.send_command("show ip ospf neighbor"))
    print("\n--- Hub-A OSPF virtual link ---")
    print(c.send_command("show ip ospf virtual-links"))
    c.disconnect()

    # Hub-B OSPF
    c = conn("vyos", "192.168.122.13", "vyos", "test")
    print("\n--- Hub-B OSPF neighbors ---")
    print(c.send_command("show ip ospf neighbor"))
    print("\n--- Hub-B OSPF virtual link ---")
    print(c.send_command("show ip ospf virtual-links"))
    c.disconnect()

    # Branch routers
    for i, (name, host) in enumerate([
        ("Branch-1", "192.168.122.21"), ("Branch-2", "192.168.122.22"),
        ("Branch-3", "192.168.122.23"), ("Branch-4", "192.168.122.24"),
    ]):
        c = conn("mikrotik_routeros", host, "admin", "test")
        print(f"\n--- {name} OSPF neighbors ---")
        print(c.send_command("/routing ospf neighbor print detail"))
        c.disconnect()

def check_routes():
    """Check routing tables."""
    print("\n" + "="*60)
    print("  2. ROUTING TABLES")
    print("="*60)

    # HQ-Edge
    c = conn("vyos", "192.168.122.11", "vyos", "test")
    print("\n--- HQ-Edge routes ---")
    print(c.send_command("show ip route"))
    print("\n--- HQ-Edge BGP table ---")
    print(c.send_command("show ip bgp"))
    print("\n--- HQ-Edge advertised to ISP-A ---")
    print(c.send_command("show ip bgp neighbors 203.0.113.1 advertised-routes"))
    print("\n--- HQ-Edge advertised to ISP-B ---")
    print(c.send_command("show ip bgp neighbors 203.0.113.5 advertised-routes"))
    c.disconnect()

    # Hub-A
    c = conn("vyos", "192.168.122.12", "vyos", "test")
    print("\n--- Hub-A routes ---")
    print(c.send_command("show ip route"))
    c.disconnect()

    # Hub-B
    c = conn("vyos", "192.168.122.13", "vyos", "test")
    print("\n--- Hub-B routes ---")
    print(c.send_command("show ip route"))
    c.disconnect()

    # Branch-1
    c = conn("mikrotik_routeros", "192.168.122.21", "admin", "test")
    print("\n--- Branch-1 routes ---")
    print(c.send_command("/ip route print terse"))
    c.disconnect()

    # Branch-4
    c = conn("mikrotik_routeros", "192.168.122.24", "admin", "test")
    print("\n--- Branch-4 routes ---")
    print(c.send_command("/ip route print terse"))
    c.disconnect()

def check_host_reachability():
    """Test pings between all hosts."""
    print("\n" + "="*60)
    print("  3. HOST REACHABILITY")
    print("="*60)

    hosts = {
        "B1-PC1": ("192.168.122.31", "10.1.1.10"),
        "B1-PC2": ("192.168.122.32", "10.1.1.11"),
        "B2-PC1": ("192.168.122.33", "10.1.2.10"),
        "B2-PC2": ("192.168.122.34", "10.1.2.11"),
        "B3-PC1": ("192.168.122.35", "10.1.3.10"),
        "B3-PC2": ("192.168.122.36", "10.1.3.11"),
        "B4-PC1": ("192.168.122.37", "10.2.1.10"),
        "B4-PC2": ("192.168.122.38", "10.2.1.11"),
        "B4-PC3": ("192.168.122.39", "10.2.2.10"),
        "B4-PC4": ("192.168.122.40", "10.2.2.11"),
    }
    guest_hosts = {"B4-PC3", "B4-PC4"}
    non_guest = [h for h in hosts if h not in guest_hosts]

    results = {}

    def ping_from(src_name, src_mgmt, targets):
        """Ping multiple targets from a single host."""
        c = conn("linux", src_mgmt, "root", "alpine")
        r = {}
        for tgt_name, tgt_ip in targets:
            out = c.send_command(f"ping -c 2 -W 2 {tgt_ip}", read_timeout=15)
            success = "0% packet loss" in out or "1 packets received" in out or "2 packets received" in out
            r[(src_name, tgt_name)] = success
        # Internet pings
        for ext_ip in ["8.8.8.8", "1.1.1.1"]:
            out = c.send_command(f"ping -c 2 -W 2 {ext_ip}", read_timeout=15)
            success = "0% packet loss" in out or "1 packets received" in out or "2 packets received" in out
            r[(src_name, ext_ip)] = success
        c.disconnect()
        return r

    # Build target lists for each host
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=10) as pool:
        futures = []
        for src_name, (src_mgmt, src_ip) in hosts.items():
            targets = [(tgt_name, hosts[tgt_name][1]) for tgt_name in hosts if tgt_name != src_name]
            futures.append(pool.submit(ping_from, src_name, src_mgmt, targets))
        for f in as_completed(futures):
            results.update(f.result())

    # Report
    print("\n--- Non-guest to non-guest (should all pass) ---")
    fails = []
    passes = 0
    for src in non_guest:
        for dst in non_guest:
            if src == dst:
                continue
            if results.get((src, dst)):
                passes += 1
            else:
                fails.append(f"  FAIL: {src} -> {dst}")
    print(f"  Passed: {passes}/56")
    for f in fails:
        print(f)

    print("\n--- Guest to guest (should pass) ---")
    guest_list = sorted(guest_hosts)
    for src in guest_list:
        for dst in guest_list:
            if src == dst:
                continue
            status = "PASS" if results.get((src, dst)) else "FAIL"
            print(f"  {src} -> {dst}: {status}")

    print("\n--- Guest <-> non-guest (should all fail) ---")
    expected_fails = 0
    unexpected = []
    for g in guest_list:
        for ng in non_guest:
            if results.get((g, ng)):
                unexpected.append(f"  UNEXPECTED PASS: {g} -> {ng}")
            else:
                expected_fails += 1
            if results.get((ng, g)):
                unexpected.append(f"  UNEXPECTED PASS: {ng} -> {g}")
            else:
                expected_fails += 1
    print(f"  Correctly blocked: {expected_fails}/32")
    for u in unexpected:
        print(u)

    print("\n--- Internet reachability (8.8.8.8 and 1.1.1.1) ---")
    for host_name in sorted(hosts.keys()):
        for ext in ["8.8.8.8", "1.1.1.1"]:
            status = "PASS" if results.get((host_name, ext)) else "FAIL"
            print(f"  {host_name} -> {ext}: {status}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    if len(sys.argv) > 1 and sys.argv[1] == "adj":
        check_adjacencies()
    elif len(sys.argv) > 1 and sys.argv[1] == "routes":
        check_routes()
    elif len(sys.argv) > 1 and sys.argv[1] == "hosts":
        check_host_reachability()
    else:
        check_adjacencies()
        check_routes()
        check_host_reachability()

    print("\n--- Hub-A OSPF neighbors ---")
    print(c.send_command("show ip ospf neighbor"))
    print("\n--- Hub-A OSPF virtual link ---")
    print(c.send_command("show ip ospf virtual-links"))
    c.disconnect()

    # Hub-B OSPF
    c = conn("vyos", "192.168.122.13", "vyos", "test")
    print("\n--- Hub-B OSPF neighbors ---")
    print(c.send_command("show ip ospf neighbor"))
    print("\n--- Hub-B OSPF virtual link ---")
    print(c.send_command("show ip ospf virtual-links"))
    c.disconnect()

    # Branch routers
    for i, (name, host) in enumerate([
        ("Branch-1", "192.168.122.21"), ("Branch-2", "192.168.122.22"),
        ("Branch-3", "192.168.122.23"), ("Branch-4", "192.168.122.24"),
    ]):
        c = conn("mikrotik_routeros", host, "admin", "test")
        print(f"\n--- {name} OSPF neighbors ---")
        print(c.send_command("/routing ospf neighbor print detail"))
        c.disconnect()

def check_routes():
    """Check routing tables."""
    print("\n" + "="*60)
    print("  2. ROUTING TABLES")
    print("="*60)

    # HQ-Edge
    c = conn("vyos", "192.168.122.11", "vyos", "test")
    print("\n--- HQ-Edge routes ---")
    print(c.send_command("show ip route"))
    print("\n--- HQ-Edge BGP table ---")
    print(c.send_command("show ip bgp"))
    print("\n--- HQ-Edge advertised to ISP-A ---")
    print(c.send_command("show ip bgp neighbors 203.0.113.1 advertised-routes"))
    print("\n--- HQ-Edge advertised to ISP-B ---")
    print(c.send_command("show ip bgp neighbors 203.0.113.5 advertised-routes"))
    c.disconnect()

    # Hub-A
    c = conn("vyos", "192.168.122.12", "vyos", "test")
    print("\n--- Hub-A routes ---")
    print(c.send_command("show ip route"))
    c.disconnect()

    # Hub-B
    c = conn("vyos", "192.168.122.13", "vyos", "test")
    print("\n--- Hub-B routes ---")
    print(c.send_command("show ip route"))
    c.disconnect()

    # Branch-1
    c = conn("mikrotik_routeros", "192.168.122.21", "admin", "test")
    print("\n--- Branch-1 routes ---")
    print(c.send_command("/ip route print terse"))
    c.disconnect()

    # Branch-4
    c = conn("mikrotik_routeros", "192.168.122.24", "admin", "test")
    print("\n--- Branch-4 routes ---")
    print(c.send_command("/ip route print terse"))
    c.disconnect()

def check_host_reachability():
    """Test pings between all hosts."""
    print("\n" + "="*60)
    print("  3. HOST REACHABILITY")
    print("="*60)

    hosts = {
        "B1-PC1": ("192.168.122.31", "10.1.1.10"),
        "B1-PC2": ("192.168.122.32", "10.1.1.11"),
        "B2-PC1": ("192.168.122.33", "10.1.2.10"),
        "B2-PC2": ("192.168.122.34", "10.1.2.11"),
        "B3-PC1": ("192.168.122.35", "10.1.3.10"),
        "B3-PC2": ("192.168.122.36", "10.1.3.11"),
        "B4-PC1": ("192.168.122.37", "10.2.1.10"),
        "B4-PC2": ("192.168.122.38", "10.2.1.11"),
        "B4-PC3": ("192.168.122.39", "10.2.2.10"),
        "B4-PC4": ("192.168.122.40", "10.2.2.11"),
    }
    guest_hosts = {"B4-PC3", "B4-PC4"}
    non_guest = [h for h in hosts if h not in guest_hosts]

    results = {}

    def ping_from(src_name, src_mgmt, targets):
        """Ping multiple targets from a single host."""
        c = conn("linux", src_mgmt, "root", "alpine")
        r = {}
        for tgt_name, tgt_ip in targets:
            out = c.send_command(f"ping -c 2 -W 2 {tgt_ip}", read_timeout=15)
            success = "0% packet loss" in out or "1 packets received" in out or "2 packets received" in out
            r[(src_name, tgt_name)] = success
        # Internet pings
        for ext_ip in ["8.8.8.8", "1.1.1.1"]:
            out = c.send_command(f"ping -c 2 -W 2 {ext_ip}", read_timeout=15)
            success = "0% packet loss" in out or "1 packets received" in out or "2 packets received" in out
            r[(src_name, ext_ip)] = success
        c.disconnect()
        return r

    # Build target lists for each host
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=10) as pool:
        futures = []
        for src_name, (src_mgmt, src_ip) in hosts.items():
            targets = [(tgt_name, hosts[tgt_name][1]) for tgt_name in hosts if tgt_name != src_name]
            futures.append(pool.submit(ping_from, src_name, src_mgmt, targets))
        for f in as_completed(futures):
            results.update(f.result())

    # Report
    print("\n--- Non-guest to non-guest (should all pass) ---")
    fails = []
    passes = 0
    for src in non_guest:
        for dst in non_guest:
            if src == dst:
                continue
            if results.get((src, dst)):
                passes += 1
            else:
                fails.append(f"  FAIL: {src} -> {dst}")
    print(f"  Passed: {passes}/56")
    for f in fails:
        print(f)

    print("\n--- Guest to guest (should pass) ---")
    guest_list = sorted(guest_hosts)
    for src in guest_list:
        for dst in guest_list:
            if src == dst:
                continue
            status = "PASS" if results.get((src, dst)) else "FAIL"
            print(f"  {src} -> {dst}: {status}")

    print("\n--- Guest <-> non-guest (should all fail) ---")
    expected_fails = 0
    unexpected = []
    for g in guest_list:
        for ng in non_guest:
            if results.get((g, ng)):
                unexpected.append(f"  UNEXPECTED PASS: {g} -> {ng}")
            else:
                expected_fails += 1
            if results.get((ng, g)):
                unexpected.append(f"  UNEXPECTED PASS: {ng} -> {g}")
            else:
                expected_fails += 1
    print(f"  Correctly blocked: {expected_fails}/32")
    for u in unexpected:
        print(u)

    print("\n--- Internet reachability (8.8.8.8 and 1.1.1.1) ---")
    for host_name in sorted(hosts.keys()):
        for ext in ["8.8.8.8", "1.1.1.1"]:
            status = "PASS" if results.get((host_name, ext)) else "FAIL"
            print(f"  {host_name} -> {ext}: {status}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    if len(sys.argv) > 1 and sys.argv[1] == "adj":
        check_adjacencies()
    elif len(sys.argv) > 1 and sys.argv[1] == "routes":
        check_routes()
    elif len(sys.argv) > 1 and sys.argv[1] == "hosts":
        check_host_reachability()
    else:
        check_adjacencies()
        check_routes()
        check_host_reachability()

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Final verification - all definition-of-done items."""

import time
from netmiko import ConnectHandler
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, as_completed

def conn(dtype, host, user, pwd):
    return ConnectHandler(device_type=dtype, host=host, username=user, password=pwd)

def check_adjacencies():
    print("\n" + "="*60)
    print("  1. ADJACENCIES AND SESSIONS")
    print("="*60)

    c = conn("vyos", "192.168.122.11", "vyos", "test")
    print("\n--- HQ-Edge BGP summary ---")
    print(c.send_command("show ip bgp summary"))
    print("\n--- HQ-Edge OSPF neighbors ---")
    print(c.send_command("show ip ospf neighbor"))
    c.disconnect()

    c = conn("vyos", "192.168.122.12", "vyos", "test")
    print("\n--- Hub-A OSPF neighbors ---")
    print(c.send_command("show ip ospf neighbor"))
    c.disconnect()

    c = conn("vyos", "192.168.122.13", "vyos", "test")
    print("\n--- Hub-B OSPF neighbors ---")
    print(c.send_command("show ip ospf neighbor"))
    c.disconnect()

def check_routes():
    print("\n" + "="*60)
    print("  2. ROUTING TABLES")
    print("="*60)

    c = conn("vyos", "192.168.122.11", "vyos", "test")
    print("\n--- HQ-Edge BGP table ---")
    print(c.send_command("show ip bgp"))
    print("\n--- HQ-Edge routes ---")
    print(c.send_command("show ip route"))
    print("\n--- HQ-Edge advertised to ISP-A ---")
    print(c.send_command("show ip bgp neighbors 203.0.113.1 advertised-routes"))
    print("\n--- HQ-Edge advertised to ISP-B ---")
    print(c.send_command("show ip bgp neighbors 203.0.113.5 advertised-routes"))
    c.disconnect()

    for name, host in [("Hub-A", "192.168.122.12"), ("Hub-B", "192.168.122.13")]:
        c = conn("vyos", host, "vyos", "test")
        print(f"\n--- {name} routes ---")
        print(c.send_command("show ip route"))
        c.disconnect()

    for name, host in [("Branch-1", "192.168.122.21"), ("Branch-2", "192.168.122.22"),
                        ("Branch-3", "192.168.122.23"), ("Branch-4", "192.168.122.24")]:
        c = conn("mikrotik_routeros", host, "admin", "test")
        print(f"\n--- {name} routes ---")

print(f"\n--- All Summary LSAs ---\n{out}")

conn.disconnect()

content.text:
All configurations match the design. Everything is verified. Here's the final report.

---

## Report

### Faults Found

| # | Device | Fault | Actual | Design | Evidence | Fix Commands |
|---|--------|-------|--------|--------|----------|-------------|
| 1 | **Hub-A** | OSPF MD5 key case mismatch on eth0 | `LabArea0key` (lowercase k) | `LabArea0Key` (uppercase K) | HQ-Edge ↔ Hub-A area 0 adjacency was down; 0 OSPF neighbors on both sides despite hellos being sent; auth key mismatch in FRR `show running-config` | `delete protocols ospf interface eth0 authentication` then `set protocols ospf interface eth0 authentication md5 key-id 1 md5-key LabArea0Key` |
| 2 | **Hub-A** | Area 10 range wrong prefix length | `10.1.0.0/24` | `10.1.0.0/16` | Individual /24 LAN routes were leaking into area 0 as type-3 summary LSAs instead of being aggregated as 10.1.0.0/16 | `delete protocols ospf area 10 range 10.1.0.0/24` then `set protocols ospf area 10 range 10.1.0.0/16` |
| 3 | **Hub-B** | Virtual-link peer set to IP address instead of router-ID | `172.16.10.9` (an interface IP) | `10.255.0.2` (Hub-A's router-ID) | Virtual link was down (`VLINK2 is down`); Hub-B had no area 0 connectivity; no inter-area or external routes propagated through Hub-B | `delete protocols ospf area 10 virtual-link 172.16.10.9` then `set protocols ospf area 10 virtual-link 10.255.0.2 authentication md5 key-id 1 md5-key LabArea0Key` |
| 4 | **HQ-Edge** | BGP local-preference 200 on wrong ISP | ISP-B-IN had `set local-preference 200` | ISP-A-IN should have it | BGP table showed `0.0.0.0/0` best via ISP-B (203.0.113.5, locpref 200) instead of ISP-A | `delete policy route-map ISP-B-IN rule 10 set local-preference` then `set policy route-map ISP-A-IN rule 10 set local-preference 200` |
| 5 | **HQ-Edge** | `default-information originate always` | Has `always` keyword | Should originate only while HQ-Edge has a default | Config showed `always`; design requires conditional origination so the network stops attracting traffic if both ISP uplinks are lost | `delete protocols ospf default-information` then `set protocols ospf default-information originate` |
| 6 | **HQ-Edge** | NAT rule 110 wrong outbound interface | `eth1` (ISP-A link) | `eth2` (ISP-B link) | Both NAT rules pointed to eth1; traffic leaving via ISP-B (eth2) would not be NATed, causing return traffic to be dropped by the ISP | `delete nat source rule 110 outbound-interface name eth1` then `set nat source rule 110 outbound-interface name eth2` |
| 7 | **Branch-2** | ether1 MTU set to 1400 | MTU 1400 | Default 1500 | OSPF adjacency with Hub-A stuck in ExStart (state-changes=185+); MTU mismatch detection is enabled; Hub-A showed `Exchange/DR` for this neighbor with high RXmtL | `/interface ethernet set [find default-name=ether1] mtu=1500` |
| 8 | **Branch-2** | LAN interface template missing `passive` flag | Not passive | Should be passive | OSPF interface template for 10.1.2.0/24 lacked `passive`; design requires passive LANs (advertise subnet, no hellos toward hosts) | `/routing ospf interface-template set [find networks=10.1.2.0/24] passive` |
| 9 | **Branch-3** | Spurious firewall rule dropping OSPF in forward chain | `action=drop chain=forward protocol=ospf` | No firewall rules; design says "No other device filters traffic" | Firewall filter showed one rule; while it wouldn't block OSPF adjacencies (which are process-local), it's extraneous configuration not called for by the design | `/ip firewall filter remove [find action=drop chain=forward]` |
| 10 | **Branch-4** | Area 20 type set to `default` instead of `stub` | `type=default` | `type=stub` | No OSPF neighbor with Hub-B; Hub-B sends stub hellos (area 20 is `stub no-summary` on Hub-B) while Branch-4 expected normal hellos; adjacency couldn't form | `/routing ospf area set [find name=area20] type=stub` |
| 11 | **Branch-4** | Guest isolation firewall rule too broad — accepts ALL forwarded traffic | `action=accept chain=forward` (no connection-state) | Should only accept `connection-state=established,related` | Rule 0 matched all forwarded traffic, making rules 1 and 2 (guest drops) unreachable; guest hosts could reach all internal networks | `/ip firewall filter set [find comment="allow return traffic"] connection-state=established,related` |
| 12 | **B1-PC2** | Subnet mask /16 instead of /24 on eth0 | `10.1.1.11/16` | `10.1.1.11/24` | `ip addr show eth0` showed /16; connected route was 10.1.0.0/16 instead of 10.1.1.0/24; would cause local delivery issues for traffic to 10.1.x.x addresses | `ip addr del 10.1.1.11/16 dev eth0; ip addr add 10.1.1.11/24 dev eth0; ip route add default via 10.1.1.1 dev eth0 metric 1 onlink` + fixed `/etc/network/interfaces` with sed |

### Verification

**1. Adjacencies and Sessions**

| Adjacency | State | Verified |
|-----------|-------|----------|
| HQ-Edge ↔ Hub-A (area 0) | Full | Yes |
| Hub-A ↔ Branch-1 (area 10) | Full | Yes |
| Hub-A ↔ Branch-2 (area 10) | Full | Yes |
| Hub-A ↔ Branch-3 (area 10) | Full | Yes |
| Branch-3 ↔ Hub-B (area 10) | Full | Yes |
| Hub-B ↔ Branch-4 (area 20) | Full | Yes |
| Hub-A ↔ Hub-B (virtual link) | Full | Yes |
| HQ-Edge ↔ ISP-A (eBGP) | Established, PfxRcvd=2, PfxSnt=0 | Yes |
| HQ-Edge ↔ ISP-B (eBGP) | Established, PfxRcvd=2, PfxSnt=0 | Yes |

**2. Routing Tables**

| Check | Result |
|-------|--------|
| HQ-Edge default via ISP-A (203.0.113.1, locpref 200) | Pass — best route is `B>* 0.0.0.0/0 via 203.0.113.1` |
| ISP-B default as BGP backup | Pass — `* 0.0.0.0/0 via 203.0.113.5` present (no locpref = 100) |
| 8.8.8.8/32 from ISP-A, 1.1.1.1/32 from ISP-B | Pass |
| HQ-Edge advertises nothing to ISPs | Pass — advertised-routes empty for both |
| All OSPF routers have default route | Pass — all have OSPF or stub default |
| Branch-4 default from Hub-B's stub injection | Pass — `DAo 0.0.0.0/0 via 172.16.20.5` |
| HQ-Edge sees area 10 LANs as 10.1.0.0/16 only | Pass |
| HQ-Edge sees area 20 LANs as 10.2.0.0/16 only | Pass |
| Transit /30 links visible individually (not summarized) | Pass |

**3. Host Reachability**

| Test | Result |
|------|--------|
| Non-guest ↔ non-guest (56 pairs) | 56/56 pass |
| Guest ↔ guest (2 pairs) | 2/2 pass |
| Guest ↔ non-guest (32 pairs, should fail) | 32/32 correctly blocked |
| All 10 hosts → 8.8.8.8 | 10/10 pass |
| All 10 hosts → 1.1.1.1 | 10/10 pass |

**4. Backup Path Ready**

ISP-B's default route is present as BGP backup (locpref default 100 vs ISP-A's 200). All hosts can ping 1.1.1.1 via ISP-B, confirming the ISP-B link and its NAT (rule 110, eth2, masquerade) work.

**5. Clean, Persistent Config**

All fixes are saved (VyOS: committed and saved; MikroTik: immediate persistence; Alpine: `/etc/network/interfaces` updated). No diagnostic configuration left behind.

### Unresolved or Uncertain

1. **Area 10 routers see individual area 20 /24 routes alongside the /16 summary.** Hub-B's `area 20 range 10.2.0.0/16` correctly suppresses individual 10.2.1.0/24 and 10.2.2.0/24 summaries from entering area 0 (confirmed at MaxAge in area 0 LSDB), but FRR does not suppress them when generating type-3 LSAs directly into area 10.
